title: To Be Or Not To Be
statement:
Write `expect(val)`, a tiny helper for writing tests. It takes any value `val` and returns an object with two methods, both of which compare `val` with another value using **strict** equality (`===`):

- `toBe(other)` returns `true` when `val === other`. Otherwise it throws an `Error` whose message is `"Not Equal"`.
- `notToBe(other)` returns `true` when `val !== other`. Otherwise it throws an `Error` whose message is `"Equal"`.

Each case gives `val`, the name of a `method` (`"toBe"` or `"notToBe"`) and `other`. The judge evaluates `expect(val)[method](other)` and answers `{ "value": result }` with what the method returned, or `{ "error": message }` with the message of the error it threw. Every value in a case is built separately from JSON, so `val` and `other` are never the same array or object, even when they look alike.
constraints: val and other are JSON values: null, a boolean, a number, a string, an array or an object
signature: Object expect(Object val, String method, Object other)
api: expect(val: unknown): { toBe(other: unknown): boolean; notToBe(other: unknown): boolean }
notes:
## Intuition

`expect(val)` returns right away, yet `val` is needed later, when `toBe` or `notToBe` is called. That is exactly what a **closure** provides: the methods of the returned object are created inside `expect`, so they keep access to its `val`. Each method is then one strict comparison, followed either by returning `true` or by throwing an error with the right message. (The brute force builds a class instance instead and tests equality with `[val].includes(other)`, which agrees with `===` on every JSON value.)

## Approach

1. `expect(val)` returns an object literal with two methods; both close over `val`.
2. `toBe(other)`: if `val !== other`, throw `new Error("Not Equal")`; otherwise return `true`.
3. `notToBe(other)`: if `val === other`, throw `new Error("Equal")`; otherwise return `true`.

## Example 1, step by step

`val = 5`, `method = "toBe"`, `other = 5`.

- `expect(5)` returns the object; its methods remember `val = 5`.
- `toBe(5)` checks `5 !== 5`, which is false, so nothing is thrown.
- It returns `true`, and the judge answers `{ "value": true }`.

In Example 2, `toBe(null)` finds `5 !== null`, throws `Error("Not Equal")`, and the answer is `{ "error": "Not Equal" }`. In Example 3, `notToBe(null)` finds `5 === null` false and returns `true`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(1) per call for numbers, booleans, `null` and object references; two strings may take O(length) to compare.
- Space: O(1): the closure keeps one value.

## Pitfalls

- Loose equality `==` is wrong here: `0 == false` and `5 == "5"` are true, but both pairs must be **Not Equal**.
- Deep equality is not wanted either: two separately built arrays `[1, 2]` are different objects, so `toBe` throws.
- Throw a real `Error` with the exact message, and return `true` on success rather than nothing.
- Keep the messages the right way round: `toBe` fails with `"Not Equal"`, `notToBe` with `"Equal"`.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `val` | the value under test, captured by the closure |
| `other` | the value a method compares `val` with |

narration.1: expect receives the value under test; the methods created below keep it through a closure.
narration.2: Return an object holding the two checks, so a caller can write expect(val).toBe(other).
narration.3: toBe passes when val and other are strictly equal.
narration.4: Strict inequality means the check fails: different types or values, or two distinct objects.
narration.5: A failed toBe throws an Error with the message "Not Equal".
narration.7: The values matched, so the check passes and reports true.
narration.9: notToBe passes when the two values are not strictly equal.
narration.10: If they are strictly equal, the check fails.
narration.11: A failed notToBe throws an Error with the message "Equal".
narration.13: The values differ, so notToBe reports true.
